claims.text: Severe plastic deformation can produce an ultrafine-grained stainless-steel microstructure.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steel has a high density of grain boundaries.
The high density of grain boundaries in ultrafine-grained stainless steel accelerates chromium diffusion.
Accelerated chromium diffusion causes enhanced chromium enrichment of the surface passivation film.
Severe-plastic-deformation-produced ultrafine-grained stainless steels generally have better corrosion resistance than coarse-grained stainless steels.
Ultrafine-grained or nanocrystalline stainless steels exhibit greater chromium enrichment in their passivation films than coarse-grained materials.
Greater chromium enrichment of the passivation film is responsible for enhanced corrosion resistance.
Ultrafine-grained stainless steel forms a chromium-rich passivation film more rapidly than coarse-grained stainless steel.
The chromium-enriched passivation film forms a more effective corrosion barrier than the passivation film on coarse-grained stainless steel.
Under identical exposure conditions, ultrafine-grained stainless steel will have a lower corrosion rate than coarse-grained stainless steel.
Chromium enrichment of passivation films in ultrafine-grained or nanocrystalline stainless steels has been experimentally observed using XPS and corrected STEM.
Acidic or aqueous aggressive media are representative of chemical-processing and nuclear-power service environments.
The proposed passivation benefit should apply broadly to chromium-containing stainless steels in chemical-processing and nuclear-power environments when no other degradation mechanism dominates.
Other degradation mechanisms induced by temperature or chemical exposure can overwhelm the passivation benefit of grain refinement.
The magnitude of corrosion-rate reduction and chromium-diffusion kinetics vary with alloy composition, grain refinement, and environmental conditions.
